Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-20

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Alex Mercer from Redwood, joining with Priya and Jonah. How are you all doing?
[00:07] Maya (Hyde): Hi Alex. Good, thanks. We got a full table so appreciate the time.
[00:10] Carlos (Hyde): Hey, yeah morning for us. Excited to see the model picklist flow, we talked about this a bit in the intro but curious to see the catalog in action.
[00:18] Alex: Great. Priya will lead the demo and Jonah will chime on catalog curation/metrics. We'll go through selecting open models, how the compatibility matrix surfaces kernel/hardware fit, and the bench workflow that ties into Redwood Optimize.
[00:30] Priya (SE): Okay, jumping in. So first screen is our model catalog. Quick note — models are annotated with performance tiers, recommended runtime (fp16, int8, awq), and typical cost per 1k tokens.
[00:45] Priya: For Hyde's chat microservice you mentioned short completions, mostly under 64 tokens, and a p50 latency target around 200ms is ideal. Correct?
[00:52] Maya: Correct. We have a hard requirement for sub-200ms p50 for user-initiated chat, else product team flags it as poor experience.
[00:58] Priya: Cool. So I'll filter catalog for models that are optimized for short context and low latency and then open the compatibility matrix card.
[01:10] [01:10] Priya: (clicks) Here you can see kernel mappings per hardware — e.g., A100 vs H100 vs rtx-8000 type, and the quantization path. Note that some older LLMs only have fp16 support and those won't be great at int8 size savings.
[01:30] Carlos: Sorry, quick Q — when you say kernel mapping, is that auto-detected per model or we can override? We have some in-house builds and want to ensure our bespoke kernels get used.
[01:38] Priya: Good question — we auto-scan the model artifact and recommend a kernel and quant profile. You can override in the deployment config if you bring a custom runtime. For private/on-prem we also support bringing your own kernel, but the catalog shows Redwood-verified defaults.
[01:52] Samir (SRE): Are the kernel selections deterministic? We've seen flip-flopping in other systems where small library changes change perf a lot.
[01:58] Priya: We lock kernel selection per model-version as part of the rollout. The matrix shows the recommended kernel + a confidence score. If a kernel change occurs we create a diffed release and flag regressions. That's part of our model lifecycle ops.
[02:12] Jonah (Product): Also worth noting the catalog keeps historical bench snapshots — you can compare p50/p95 token latencies across versions and hardware in the same table.
[02:22] Maya: Can you show an example of selecting three models and creating a bench run?
[02:25] Priya: Sure. I'm selecting Mistral-derived-12B-open (fake name for example), a Llama-2-13b variant, and a quantized 7b optimized for int8. Naming in the UI is shorthand but each has a detail page with bench traces.
[02:36] [02:36] Priya: (opens bench modal) Here we create a bench request. We can upload workload traces or select a sample prompt set. For Hyde I'd recommend using your chat workload trace — it preserves length distribution and burstiness.
[02:50] Carlos: We can provide 48 hours of anonymized logs, is that sufficient?
[02:53] Priya: Yep, that should be plenty. We typically ask for at least 10k short completions or representative sample; 48 hours sounds great. We'll run bench across hosted and dedicated profiles unless you want private only.
[03:06] Maya: We need to evaluate private deployment too — data residency and KMS are big here. Ellen, any concerns?
[03:12] Ellen (Security): We require SOC 2 attestation, SSO with SAML, and customer-managed KMS keys for any private storage. Also strict audit logs and retention control.
[03:21] Alex: That's in line with our Redwood Private offering. We support BYOK via customer KMS/HSM and full audit logs. We have a SOC2 report we can share.
[03:29] Ellen: Great. Can you show where those options live in the console?
[03:33] Priya: Sure — under deployment settings we have a toggles page: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. For Private there are additional controls: KMS ARN input, SSO config link, and audit retention slider.
[03:43] [03:43] Priya: (navigates) If you click 'Security integrations' here you can test SAML metadata import and then map RBAC roles.
[03:50] Ellen: RBAC mapping looks helpful. Do you tie logs to the customer audit trail or to a Redwood-managed index?
[03:57] Priya: Logs are shipped to a customer-managed bucket for Private; for hosted we retain logs in our system with configurable retention. All access is logged and visible in the Console's audit view.
[04:08] Carlos: Back to bench — how do you measure cost? We need to estimate token cost since our chat has high aggregate volume.
[04:14] Jonah: Bench results include a cost projection based on your token distribution and the model's measured throughput and tail latency. We show per-1k-token cost under each deployment mode and include batching/caching effects.
[04:26] Maya: About batching — our UX folks worry about latency spikes with batching aggregation. Will batching break the 200ms p50 goal?
[04:33] Priya: Bench mode simulates your arrival distribution. If the workload is spiky with low QPS per user, batching may not trigger much. We also support continuous prefix caching which helps for many chat use cases — that reduces tokens generated and avoids batching-induced latency increases.
[04:48] [04:48] Samir: Could you explain prefix caching again? We use KV cache internally but not at the platform level.
[04:53] Priya: Prefix caching stores repeated prompt prefixes (like system and recent context) and reuses corresponding KV side effects to avoid re-computing the entire attention for common prefixes. It's most effective when prompts share system instructions or templates.
[05:07] Maya: Makes sense. For our chat flows, system prompts are static, so could be useful.
[05:11] Priya: Exactly. We'll surface cache hit rate estimates in bench results too.
[05:18] [05:18] Carlos: On compatibility matrix — does it show memory footprint per quant profile? We want to ensure the selected model fits on our target GPUs for dedicated.
[05:25] Priya: Yes, the matrix shows peak VRAM, expected KV cache size per sequence length, and recommended batch sizes per GPU type. There's also a 'fit' column that shows whether a model will fit given a chosen hardware slab.
[05:36] Jonah: We also include kernel-level speedups and an estimated perf delta when switching from fp16 to int8/awq. That helps with cost tradeoffs.
[05:45] Maya: Can you annotate which models are Redwood-verified for accuracy/regression risk? We care about quality guardrails as well.
[05:51] Priya: We tag models with a quality score derived from eval suites and our continuous quality monitoring. There's also a playbook entry that lists recommended prompt sets to use for regression checks.
[06:04] [06:04] Maya: Any examples of tradeoffs where a smaller model beats a larger one for UX?
[06:09] Jonah: Sure — for short completions, a well-quantized 7b can meet latency and token-cost targets and may actually give higher effective throughput due to lower kv cache overhead. Larger models sometimes only help on longer-context tasks.
[06:21] Ellen: About private deployments, what network topology do you support? VPC peering, private link, or on-prem?
[06:28] Alex: We support three topologies: VPC peering, PrivateLink-style endpoints, and full on-prem bundle for air-gapped. Each option includes a control-plane connection that can be customer-managed.
[06:39] Carlos: Good. On the bench run, would Redwood run on our AWS account or on Redwood infra? We prefer tests on our infra to catch environment variances.
[06:47] Priya: We can do both — hosted bench on Redwood infra for speed and a dedicated/private bench that runs in your account or in a controlled private environment. For strict fidelity we recommend a dedicated run in your account.
[06:58] Maya: Ok let's assume we want runs in our account. What level of access do you need?
[07:02] Priya: We'll provide an infra playbook. Typically we need a short-lived role with permissions to create VMs/ECS tasks and attach GPUs, and a S3 bucket for log output. We'll provide a CloudFormation/Terraform template.
[07:14] [07:14] Samir: Any compliance gating for those roles? We can't give persistent admin rights.
[07:18] Alex: Absolutely — we only request scoped, short-lived roles. We support IRSA and assume-role patterns. The bench runner will drop artifacts into your S3 and only run ephemeral instances.
[07:29] Maya: Thanks. Can we talk about routing and fallback? If the primary model gets overloaded, what happens?
[07:33] Priya: Redwood Smart Routing allows policy-based fallbacks — e.g., for p95 SLO breaches, traffic can route to a cheaper/less accurate variant or region. You can set per-route fallbacks and an automatic rollback.
[07:46] Carlos: Will fallback change the response shape or content noticeably? Our client expects structured JSON from the model.
[07:52] Priya: For structured outputs we recommend preserving the call signature and using function-calling or constrained-output models. The fallback variants should be compatible; the console flags API compatibility and function schemas.
[08:05] [08:05] Maya: Good. Any latency numbers you can show for the three example models?
[08:08] Priya: Right now the bench preview shows p50/p95 for A100 hosted: 7b-int8 -> p50 95ms, p95 280ms; 13b-fp16 -> p50 180ms, p95 630ms; 12b-mistral-> p50 140ms, p95 420ms. Note these are synthetic hosted numbers — we'll run your workload to get real ones.
[08:30] Samir: That 13b p95 is rough, so for tight UX we might prefer 7b quant or a 12b optimized.
[08:36] Priya: Exactly. Bench will show tradeoffs including hit-rate for prefix cache which can drop p95 significantly for chat.
[08:44] Jonah: Also, we can run per-token cost sim with and without prefix caching to give your finance team accurate projections.
[08:52] Maya: Two more security Qs — encryption at rest for model artifacts and key rotation cadence?
[08:58] Ellen: (overlap) We have to ensure model checkpoints aren't accessible by third parties and that keys rotate quarterly.
[09:03] Alex: For Private we put the model artifacts in your KMS-protected bucket; key rotation is customer-managed. For Hosted we use instance-level disk encryption and manage keys, but for enterprise deals we offer a KMS bring-your-own-key option that allows rotation policies.
[09:18] Ellen: For audit we need immutable logs for six months.
[09:22] Priya: Console audit retention is configurable; we can push logs to your S3 with immutability rules.
[09:28] [09:28] Maya: Great. Back to the catalog — is there an exportable CSV of shortlisted models and bench parameters we can hand to procurement?
[09:35] Priya: Yes, catalog exports include model metadata, compatibility matrix snapshots, and bench requests. We'll attach that to the bench report.
[09:42] Carlos: One practical thing — do you support a heuristics-driven picklist? Like give me 3-4 recommended models for this workload automatically.
[09:49] Priya: We do. There's a Suggestion engine that, given your workload profile and constraints (latency target, max cost per 1k tokens, preferred hardware), ranks candidates and outputs a picklist. You can then bench the top N.
[10:02] Maya: Can that suggestion be constrained to open models only? We need license clarity.
[10:06] Priya: Yes, filter by license type. We label model licenses in the catalog (Apache, MIT, proprietary, etc.).
[10:12] Jonah: For your pilot I'd recommend the autopick with open-model filter, then one larger L2-style model for quality baseline.
[10:19] [10:19] Maya: Perfect. For procurement we also need a cost cap estimate for the pilot. Alex, can you ballpark for 3-month pilot with moderate load?
[10:25] Alex: If you run the bench with 100 QPS typical and average completion length of 40 tokens, a hosted pilot across three models could be in the low tens of thousands per month, but dedicated options change that profile. We'll follow up with a tailored estimate once we see the bench traces.
[10:40] Carlos: That's fine as a placeholder.
[10:43] Ellen: Also add a line for security review costs if you need on-site audits.
[10:47] Alex: Noted.
[10:50] [10:50] Priya: Quickly demoing a bench result page — we have a timeline view, heatmap of p95 spikes, and a per-prompt latency histogram. You can click into problem prompts and see the full token trace.
[11:02] Priya: Here's the 'compatibility diff' view — it shows perf delta when moving from one kernel to another and estimated regression risk. We also surface which quant methods were tested (GPTQ, AWQ).
[11:14] Samir: Do you run real kernel-level profiling or just simulated estimates?
[11:18] Priya: For hosted/dedicated we run real profiling on the target hardware. For private we can run a local profiling agent if you allow bench in your account.
[11:27] Maya: Good. Any notes about licensing for AWQ or other quant tools?
[11:31] Jonah: We surface licenses and note third-party library constraints. We won't include any tool that is incompatible with your license preferences in the suggestion list.
[11:40] [11:40] Maya: OK — let's capture the concrete pilot plan: 1) Redwood runs bench on our workloads in our account across three open models (7b-int8, 12b-optimized, 13b-fp16 baseline), 2) evaluate p50/p95 and cache hit rates, 3) cost projection and routing policy recommendations, 4) security review. Anything to add?
[11:58] Alex: Add a short regression suite run using your sample prompts to check outputs for quality drift.
[12:03] Maya: Yes please. We'll include a handful of business-critical prompts.
[12:07] Carlos: Timing — can we target bench week of Mar 9?
[12:10] Priya: That works for us. We'll need the workload traces and temporary role by Mar 2 to provision.
[12:17] [12:17] Ellen: I'll send the compliance constraints doc today.
[12:20] Maya: Great.
[12:22] Alex: Any other blockers or questions?
[12:24] Samir: One more: what happens if the bench shows that none of the open models meet p95 threshold? Do you recommend custom fine-tuning or routing changes?
[12:33] Priya: We propose a few mitigations: a) try prefix caching + batching tweaks, b) switch to a quantization profile with less aggressive weight compression, c) recommend a dedicated slab with lower contention, or d) fallback to a slightly larger model but use constrained prompt templates. Fine-tuning is on the table if quality is the blocker.
[12:50] Maya: Good. That's what we needed.
[12:53] Alex: Alright, quick recap of next steps: Alex sends pricing and contract; Priya sends bench playbook and infra templates; Ellen sends compliance doc. We'll schedule the bench for week of Mar 9 pending artifacts.
[13:09] Maya: Thanks everyone. Looking forward to the bench.
[13:12] Alex: Thanks all. We'll follow up via email with the artifacts and onboarding steps.
